questions.q: Define resistivity and state its SI unit.
questions.a: Resistivity (ρ) is the resistance of a material per unit length and per unit cross-sectional area, defined by ρ = RA/L. SI unit: ohm-metre (Ω·m). A wrong answer (e.g., "resistivity is the same as resistance") shows the student does not distinguish between the two concepts.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material have the same length but different cross-sectional areas A₁ = 2A₂. How do their resistivities compare?
questions.a: The resistivities are EQUAL because resistivity is a material property, independent of dimensions. The resistances differ (R₁ = R₂/2 since R = ρL/A), but ρ₁ = ρ₂. A wrong answer (e.g., "ρ₁ = 2ρ₂") shows the student confuses resistance with resistivity.

questions.q: A wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 × 10⁻⁶ m² has resistance 3.4 Ω. Find the resistivity of the material.
questions.a: ρ = RA/L = (3.4)(1 × 10⁻⁶)/2 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m. A wrong answer (e.g., ρ = 3.4 × 2/10⁻⁶) shows the student inverted the formula or misapplied the units.

questions.q: Why are alloys like nichrome used in heating elements rather than pure metals?
questions.a: Alloys like nichrome have higher resistivity than pure metals (e.g., nichrome ρ ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m vs copper ρ ≈ 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m), so they produce more heat for the same current (H = I²Rt). They also have high melting points and do not oxidise easily at high temperatures. A wrong answer (e.g., "alloys are cheaper") may be true but misses the electrical reason.

questions.q: How does the resistivity of a conductor change with temperature? Compare with a semiconductor.
questions.a: For conductors: resistivity increases with temperature (more thermal vibrations scatter electrons, increasing opposition). For semiconductors: resistivity decreases with temperature (more electrons are freed from atoms, increasing charge carriers). A wrong answer (e.g., "resistivity always increases with temperature") shows the student does not distinguish conductor and semiconductor behavior.

questions.q: A copper wire has resistance 10 Ω. It is stretched to double its length (volume constant). Find the new resistance.
questions.a: When stretched to double length with volume constant: L' = 2L, so A' = A/2 (volume = AL = A'L' is constant). New resistance R' = ρL'/A' = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4ρL/A = 4R = 40 Ω. A wrong answer (e.g., R' = 20 Ω) shows the student did not account for the area change when the wire is stretched.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ (ρ) is an intrinsic property of a material that measures how strongly it opposes the flow of electric current.
Fill in the blank: Imagine two ______ wires: one thick and short, one thin and long.
What is Resistivity (ρ)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic property of a material that measures how strongly it opposes the flow of electric current.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Resistivity (ρ)?
questions.a: Students often confuse resistance and resistivity.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can define resistivity, state the formula ρ = RA/L with correct units (Ω·m), distinguish between resistance (depends on dimensions) and resistivity (material property), explain how resistivity varies with temperature for conductors, semiconductors, and insulators, and calculate resistivity from given R, A, and L values.
